“She's doing skilled production work.”

“So were you.”

“I ate your bread.”

“My bread?” the keeper said.

“Our bread,” I corrected.

“Two copper,” Holl said.

I almost objected.

Then didn't.

“Fine.”

He put two copper on the table.

The keeper took one.

I stared at her.

“Bread,” she said.

“That was not one copper of bread.”

“Table fee.”

“You have never charged a table fee.”

“New policy.”

Holl was already closing the box.

“You're encouraging her.”

“Yes.”

“Get out.”

He stood.

At the door he looked back.

“Same lot. Sample clear calls too.”

“Yes.”

“Don't change Iris yet.”

“Correct.”

“Ask customers what happens if they're wrong.”

“Approximately.”

He nodded.

Then he left with his stones and bad columns.

The room became quiet again.

I looked at the remaining copper.

One copper net after extortion.

Still more than yesterday's professional income.

Yesterday's professional income had been negative.

I had paid for transport to go nowhere useful and look at yellow cloth.

Today a testing shop owner had brought work to my breakfast table because something I had asked him to record had produced a question he wanted help answering.

The two facts did not cancel each other.

That seemed important enough that I refused to write it down.

I elevated my leg on the other chair.

The keeper put another piece of bread beside me.

“Free?” I asked.

“No.”

I ate it anyway.

*

By afternoon the swelling had reduced.

Not gone. Reduced.

I stayed downstairs.

This was partly discipline and partly because the stairs had become less interesting now that I knew I could use them under controlled conditions. Competence had ruined a perfectly good obsession.

I reread Holl's numbers from memory.

That was a mistake.

I did not have the papers.

Good.

I could reconstruct the broad pattern but not the exact counts. Also good. It prevented me from solving a business that was currently walking away from me in a wooden box.

I opened my notebook instead.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

Below that I wrote:

HOLL: COMPARE DECISIONS, NOT JUST PEOPLE.

I stared at it.

Too neat.

I crossed out HOLL.

Then I crossed out the whole sentence.

The keeper saw me.

“Bad?”

“Annoying.”

“What was it?”

“Something true enough to become false if I liked it too much.”

She considered that.

“Sounds like you.”

“Yes.”

I turned the page.

Blank.

Good.

Someone outside shouted about onions.

A cart rolled past.

Upstairs, a door opened and shut.

My leg hurt less than it had that morning.

I had one copper from work I had not gone looking for.

I had spent yesterday on a road for no reason that would survive an invoice.

Tomorrow remained offensively unassigned.

I left the page blank.
CHAPTER 86
THE PLAYER

The blank page lasted until nearly noon.

This was longer than expected.

I had assumed tomorrow would become assigned through ordinary violence. A Guild messenger. Holl returning with numbers despite being told to collect more than six days. Antonius deciding a one-hour task had siblings. Alden throwing something at a window. The keeper inventing a fee for remaining indoors.

Nothing happened.

My residual limb was less swollen than yesterday. The road soreness had settled into the dull kind that stopped being medically interesting and became personally annoying. Dressing dry. No heat. No redness. No drainage. Right thigh still sore. Lower back better. Hands almost ordinary if I did not squeeze anything hard.

I ate breakfast.

Then more breakfast because the keeper had made too much and claimed this was somehow my problem.

Then I sat.

The city continued without consulting me.

A wagon rattled past carrying empty baskets. Someone upstairs argued about a missing stocking. Two men outside spent five full minutes disagreeing about whether a barrel belonged at the front or back of a cart, then placed it in the middle. A woman came in to ask the keeper whether she knew anyone with a room for three nights. She did. Not here.

I considered going upstairs.

No.

I considered the Guild.

Dangerous. If I went there without a purpose, I would acquire one.

Arlo and Vessa were still under explicit instructions not to receive me. Their instructions, not mine, but enforcement seemed likely.

Edrin had nothing for me.

Holl had work he needed to do without my face appearing beside it.

Antonius knew where I lived.

Lyssa was working.

Sevren was probably already somewhere else because this was the defining feature of couriers.

Jorren was at the Guild yard.

That was not a reason.

I stood.

The keeper looked over.

“Guild?”

“No.”

“Where?”

“I don't know.”

Her eyebrows went up.

I disliked being interesting before leaving the room.

“Out,” I said.

“Strong plan.”

“Yes.”

I took my crutches and left before she could charge me for it.

*

Carrow was easier when I was not trying to cross it efficiently.

This was an irritating discovery because efficiency had previously been one of walking's major advantages.

With two crutches, a missing left foot, and no appointment, I could choose streets according to grade, crowd, surface, shade, benches, and whether a delivery wagon had converted the pavement into a temporary wall. There was no penalty for arriving late because there was nowhere to arrive.

I went south because the north road still existed and I did not need to prove it twice.

A baker had set cooling racks near an open window. I stopped long enough to smell bread and not buy any because I had eaten twice.

A cooper was shaving a hoop. Three children were using a gutter channel as a boat race. A dog slept with its head on a doorstep where anyone with sense would have moved it, which meant everyone stepped around the dog instead.

I did too.

At the next corner I heard somebody shout, “Too high.”

Then a hollow leather thump against wood.

Then Alden laughed.

I changed direction.

This was not an accident.

The south Guild yard had a side court I had seen before and ignored because it contained nothing worth being injured over. Today the main practice floor was occupied by shield work, so half a dozen Bronzes had migrated into the side court with two leather throwing balls, a chalked wall, and apparently no supervision.

Jorren stood with his back against the fence eating something from paper.

He saw me first.

“No.”

“I haven't asked anything.”

“You came toward Alden voluntarily.”

“That is not a question.”

“It is a diagnosis.”

Alden turned.

He had one of the leather balls in his right hand and sweat darkening the collar of his shirt.

“Greg.”

“Don't hand me the ball.”

His smile widened.

“I was going to ask if you wanted to play.”

“No.”

“Coward.”

I stopped beside Jorren.

“What is the game?”

Jorren closed his eyes.

Alden tossed the ball once and caught it.

“Three marks,” he said.

There were three chalk circles on the wall at different heights and distances from the center line. One low left. One chest-high center. One higher right.

“Rules?” I asked.

“Hit them.”

“In order?”

“Yes.”

“How many throws?”

“Three.”

“Scoring?”

“One point if you hit one.”

I waited.

Alden waited.

“That is the entire scoring system?”

“Yes.”

“No bonus for center?”

“No.”

“Distance?”

He pointed at a chalk line six paces from the wall.

“Same line.”

“Ball rotation?”

Jorren made a sound into his food.

Alden said, “You throw it.”

“Grip restrictions?”

“No.”

“Bounce permitted?”

“No.”

“Then why are there six people arguing?”

“Because Lio says the top mark is too small.”

Lio, already known to me and currently holding the second ball, said from the wall, “It is too small.”

“It is the same size it was yesterday,” Alden said.

“That does not make it good.”

This seemed reasonable.

I looked at Jorren.

“You play?”

“No.”

“Why are you here?”

“Lunch.”

He lifted the paper.

Apparently he had achieved what I was attempting.

Alden threw.

Low left. Hit.

Center. Hit.

High right.

The ball struck the chalk circle near its upper edge and dropped.

Alden turned toward me before it hit the ground.

“Three.”

“Two and a disputed boundary.”

“Chalk moved,” Alden said.

“Then your scoring surface is degrading during use.”

“Three.”

“Two.”

Lio said, “Three.”

“You just complained about the target.”

“I can dislike the target and still understand circles.”

Fair.

Alden held the ball out to me.

“No.”

“You walked over.”

“I was observing.”

“You've observed.”

I looked at the line.

Six paces.

The side court had packed dirt, reasonably flat. The wall was old timber backed by stone. The leather ball was roughly the size of my fist and stuffed enough to deform when it hit. No blades. No magic. No moving machinery. No road.

Still standing to throw would require one crutch or balancing on the right leg. Bad. Sitting would change the distance and release height. Also the chair would need to be behind the line.

I could ask for a chair.

That sounded like participation.

“No,” I said again.

Alden tossed the ball to Lio.

“Fine.”

This was unexpectedly annoying.

They played another round.

Lio hit two. A woman I knew by face but not name hit one. Another Bronze missed all three and blamed the ball. Alden hit two cleanly and one that I would have counted if I were not invested in his suffering.

I watched his shoulder.

He did not throw hard. That was the first thing.

The target was close enough that force mostly created rebound. The better throws left his hand smooth, with less visible effort than the misses. His feet did more than I expected. Small shift. Hip. Trunk. Shoulder. Release.

Old knowledge supplied a dozen throwing mechanics from weapons, stones, darts, improvised objects, and one ridiculous winter campaign involving frozen turnips.

None of those bodies were sitting down.

Interesting.

Alden caught me looking.

“Chair?”

I hated him.

“Yes.”

Jorren laughed so hard he nearly dropped lunch.

*

The chair came from the training annex.

Not a special chair. A normal wooden chair with one leg slightly shorter than the others because Carrow believed furniture should participate in uncertainty.

Alden set it behind the chalk line.

I moved it myself.

“Back another half pace,” I said.

“Why?”

“My hand starts closer to the wall than yours when seated.”

He considered that.

Then dragged the chalk line back with his heel instead.

“That works too.”

“Less furniture.”

I sat.

Crutches went on the ground to my right within reach, not leaning where somebody could kick them. Right foot flat. Left knee bent comfortably. Residual limb clear of the chair edge.

The game became different immediately.

Not harder exactly.

Different geometry.

Alden handed me the ball.

Leather. Dense stuffing. Slightly uneven seam. Enough weight to matter. Not enough to hurt the wall or anybody with reasonable luck.

“Low left,” he said.

“I know the order.”

“Wasn't sure after the questions.”

I threw.

The ball hit the wall a foot above the low circle.

Everyone became quiet for exactly long enough to be rude.

Alden said, “Good wall.”

“Shut up.”

I had thrown mostly with the arm.

Stupid.

My old body expected the left leg to receive part of the rotational shift even though I was sitting. Not weight-bearing, exactly. More like the movement map had included a base wider than the one physically available. My trunk had stopped halfway through because some part of it expected support that was not there.

That was a theory.

Observed fact: terrible throw.

I adjusted my right foot.

Center target.

Second throw hit low and right.

Better.

Third missed the high mark by less.

“Zero,” Alden said happily.

“Yes.”

“You want advice?”

“No.”

“Good. I didn't have any.”

I stood by pushing through the chair with one hand, caught myself, then stopped.

No. Why stand?

The next player could wait.

I stayed seated while Lio retrieved the balls.

Jorren came over chewing.

“You're working now.”

“I am playing.”

“You missed three times and started measuring the game.”

“It has three targets and measurable outcomes.”

“Exactly.”

“I missed all of them.”

“Yes.”

“That is offensive.”

“Good.”

Alden called, “Again?”

I said, “Yes.”

Jorren pointed his food at me.

“Game.”

“I know.”

“No notebook.”

“I didn't bring it.”

He stared.

I had not realized this until he did.

Interesting.

“No notebook,” I agreed.

Second round.

Low left.

I let my torso turn farther before release and kept the right foot planted without trying to make it replace both legs.

Hit.

The ball landed inside the chalk and bounced almost straight back.

I caught it against my chest.

Alden's expression changed.

“Accident.”

“Yes.”

Center.

Miss.

High right.

Hit edge.

“Two,” Lio said.

Alden frowned.

“That last one was boundary,” Alden said.

“Chalk moved,” I said.

Lio pointed at me.

“He learns.”

The next round became competitive.

This was not my fault.

Alden had three points. Lio had two. I had two. The unnamed woman had two and clearly did not care about any of us, which made her dangerous.

I tried more force.

Worse.

I tried less.

Better.

I changed grip.

No meaningful difference.

I moved the chair three inches left.

Alden objected.

“Line is the line.”

“The chair remains behind it.”

“You're changing position.”

“You change your feet.”

“That is different.”

“Explain.”

He opened his mouth.

Closed it.

Jorren said, “Don't help him.”

Alden kicked the chair back three inches.

I stared at him.

“Now that's interference.”

“Play.”

I played.

The low target became easy first.

Not easy. Easier.

The center target exposed timing. The high target required more shoulder and less force than I thought. When I tried to generate power from the trunk, I shifted too far left and the chair rocked.

Once.

The missing foot planted itself in my body map to catch the shift.

Nothing touched the ground.

My left hip moved anyway.

The chair tipped half an inch.

My right hand shot to the seat edge and stopped it.

The ball dropped from my other hand.

Nobody laughed.

That was worse.

“I'm fine,” I said.

Alden nodded once.

Jorren had stopped chewing.

I reset the chair.

Pessa said from behind us, “You reached past what you had.”

Of course.

I turned.

She stood at the court entrance with a practice spear over one shoulder. She was sweaty enough to have been working.

“I know,” I said.

“After.”

I disliked the accuracy.

“Yes.”

She looked at the chalk circles, the ball on the ground, my chair, then Alden.

“What is this?”

“Game,” Alden said.

Pessa looked at me.

“Game,” I said.

“Good.”

That was all.

She pointed the spear at Alden.

“You're late.”

He looked toward the main yard.

“For what?”

She smiled.

Alden stopped smiling.

“Right.”

He handed me the ball.

“Hold that.”

“No.”

He was already following Pessa.

I now held the ball.

This was how property disputes began.

Lio said, “Your throw.”

Apparently it was also how games continued.

*

Without Alden, the game improved.

Not because he was bad.

Because he was annoying enough that beating him had become the objective, and his absence returned the objective to hitting chalk with leather.

I made three.

Then one.

Then two.

The unnamed woman made three twice in a row, accepted this with no visible emotion, and left when a Guild bell sounded.

Lio made two and complained that the ball was becoming soft.

I squeezed it.

It was becoming soft.

“Stuffing shifted,” I said.

Lio said, “Don't.”

“What?”

“Turn it into work.”

“I was describing the ball.”

“Greg.”

Apparently I had a reputation.

I threw again.

Missed low.

Center hit.

High hit.

The important part was not the score.

The important part was that by then my right shoulder had begun to tire in a way I recognized before it became pain. My hands were fine. My residual limb was quiet because I had been sitting. Right thigh did almost nothing. Trunk did more.

Different cost.

I noticed it.

Then I kept playing for one more round.

Not because I had failed to notice.

Because I wanted one more round.

This distinction felt dangerously like philosophy, so I refused to examine it.

I scored one.

Terrible decision.

Worth it.

Jorren finished his lunch and finally walked over.

“My turn.”

I handed him the ball.

“You said you don't play.”

“I said I wasn't playing.”

“That was forty minutes ago.”

“Yes.”

He stood behind the line.

Low left. Hit.

Center. Hit.

High right.

Hit.

Three throws. Three clean impacts.

No wasted motion.

I stared.

Lio stared.

Jorren handed the ball back.

“You asshole,” I said.

He smiled.

“I hit people for a living.”

“That is not the same skill.”

“Apparently close enough.”

“Again.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Lunch is over.”

He walked away.

I hated friendship.

*

I left before my shoulder made the decision for me.

This was partly because I was learning.

Mostly it was because Lio needed the chair back inside and I refused to be carried with it.

Standing after sitting that long required a moment. Right foot placed. One hand on chair. One on crutch. Rise. Balance. Second crutch. Good.

The residual limb had not swollen much while I played. It noticed the first ten crutch steps afterward, though. Blood shift. Pressure. Familiar pulse.

Manageable.

The right shoulder complained from throwing, not crutching. That was new enough to be interesting.

I did not have a notebook.

Excellent.

I stopped at a food stall and bought something fried around onions because the smell defeated whatever remained of my judgment.

The vendor wrapped it in paper.

“Careful, hot.”

I put the paper between my teeth while moving both crutches three steps to the side, then sat on a low wall.

This technique lacked dignity.

It worked.

I ate.

Alden found me halfway through.

He was sweaty again, which suggested Pessa had discovered what he was late for.

“How many?” he asked.

“Three.”

His face fell.

“Once.”

“Still.”

“Jorren made three first try.”

Alden's face changed in a much more satisfying way.

“What?”

“Yes.”

“He doesn't play.”

“That was also my understanding.”

Alden looked back toward the Guild as if betrayal might still be visible through two buildings.

“I hate him.”

“Yes.”

He took a piece of my fried onion without asking.

I slapped his wrist.

He got the onion anyway.

“Tomorrow?” he asked.

I almost asked what time.

Almost asked whether Pessa was training him first, whether the court would be free, whether the chair would be available, whether the same ball would be used, whether my shoulder would recover, whether repeated seated throwing had any useful transfer to knife work, combat, balance, future prosthetic use, crutch defense, or spellcasting.

All excellent questions.

None required yet.

“Maybe,” I said.

Alden nodded.

Then he stole another onion.

This time I caught his wrist.

He twisted free.

Progress for both of us.

*

Back at lodging, the keeper looked at my empty hands.

“No work?”

“No.”

“No road?”

“No.”

“No girl?”

“Lyssa has a name.”

“So no girl.”

“No.”

She looked at my shoulder when I lowered myself into the chair.

“What did you do?”

“Played a game.”

“With what?”

“Ball.”

She waited.

I waited.

“That all?” she asked.

“Yes.”

This answer felt suspiciously incomplete.

It was also true.

She put stew in front of me.

I ate.

Afterward I opened the notebook.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

The next page was blank.

I could write shoulder fatigue.

Seated rotation.

Reach boundary.

Phantom support assumption.

Chair position.

Release angle.

Three-mark scoring distribution.

Jorren is a bastard.

That one had merit.

I picked up the pencil.

Then put it down.

Tomorrow, if I went back, I could remember how the game worked.

If I forgot something, somebody would tell me.

Probably loudly.

I closed the notebook.

My right shoulder hurt.

My left foot felt as though it was tucked under the chair even though the chair had nothing under it except floor.

I moved the chair anyway.

The sensation did not change.

Fine.

I stole bread from the kitchen.

The keeper saw me.

She did not stop me.

Three points.
CHAPTER 87
THE BLUFFER

My right shoulder objected to breakfast.

Not dramatically. It did not seize, tear, burn, or produce any of the symptoms that would justify using the word injury. It simply informed me, each time I lifted the spoon, that throwing leather balls at chalk circles had involved muscles I had not recently been using for throwing leather balls at chalk circles.

This was useful information.

It was also irritating because porridge was not heavy.

I changed hands.

The keeper watched me do it.

“No.”

“I haven’t asked anything.”

“You’re thinking about yesterday.”

“I think about most days.”

“You’re going back.”

“Maybe.”

She pointed the bread knife at my right shoulder. “No throwing.”

“I can play left-handed.”

“No.”

“That seems prejudicial.”

“That seems breakfast.”

I considered explaining that bilateral skill development had legitimate value.

Then I looked at the bread knife.

I ate.

The residual limb was better than it had been after the north road. Not normal, because normal had become a word with too many historical meanings, but the skin was dry, the swelling lower, and the deep ache from the cart had retreated into the sort of complaint that became louder only when I checked whether it was still there.

It was.

My missing left heel also itched.

That was less actionable.

By noon I had accomplished nothing except washing, eating, reading three pages of an old Guild notice I had already read, and deciding twice not to go watch Alden train.

The second decision was harder because it occurred while I was already halfway to the Guild.

I stopped at the corner.

The Guild was left.

The green door was right.

Straight ahead was a cooper arguing with a delivery boy about whether six hoops constituted a complete order when two of them were the wrong width.

I stood there long enough that the delivery boy noticed.

“Not you,” he said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Then keep it that way.”

The cooper pointed at him. “See?”

I went right.

This was maturity.

Possibly.

The green door was open despite it being too early for most of the people who treated the place as an evening destination. Nessa was behind the counter with a rag over one shoulder and an expression suggesting she had already been disappointed by several objects.

Octavia sat at the back table with four cards face down in front of her and a little pile of copper bits at her elbow.

There were two other people at the table. I knew both by face and neither by name, which was ideal. Names created obligations.

Jorren occupied a chair beside them without cards.

He had a cup.

This was also ideal.

“You’re early,” Nessa said.

“For what?”

She looked at Octavia.

Octavia looked at me.

Jorren drank.

I disliked coordinated silence.

“What?”

“Sit,” Octavia said.

“No.”

“Good. Sit.”

“That is not how that works.”

“It worked.”

I looked down.

I had already moved toward the table.

Annoying.

The chair beside Jorren was ordinary, solid, and positioned so I could get both crutches against the wall without anyone stepping on them. I sat because standing indefinitely to prove that I had not been manipulated would have been a particularly expensive form of independence.

Octavia pushed four cards toward me.

“I don’t know this game.”

“Yes.”

“That usually matters.”

“Less than you think.”

Jorren said, “It matters.”

Octavia ignored him.

I looked at the cards.

They were narrow pasteboard, worn soft at the corners, each marked with one of four suits I recognized from other Carrow games. Cups. Nails. Birds. Towers. The values ran one through nine, except apparently not all values were present in all hands, which was either because the deck was incomplete or because I did not yet understand the deal.

Probably the second.

“How much?”

“One bit to stay in,” Octavia said.

“What am I buying?”

“The right to be wrong in public.”

“That seems overpriced.”

“One bit.”

I put down one bit.

Nessa called from the counter, “He’ll pay more.”

“I heard that.”

“You were meant to.”

Octavia dealt.

The game was called Four Doors, which was already suspicious because there were no doors involved.

Each player received four cards. One stayed hidden until the end. Three could be exchanged, one at a time, through a common row in the center. The goal was not simply to make the highest total. Matching suits mattered. Pairs mattered differently. Towers broke one kind of tie. Birds broke another. A hand that looked mediocre could become strong if the hidden card matched correctly.

I asked seven questions.

Octavia answered five.

“Why won’t you answer the other two?”

“Because one is strategy.”

“And the other?”

“Also strategy.”

“That seems arbitrary.”

“Yes.”

The first hand cost me one bit.

The second cost me two because I had misunderstood how aggressively one of the unnamed men valued a visible pair of nails.

The third I folded early.

Octavia looked disappointed.

“I had nothing.”

“You had a face.”

“I generally do.”

“It was a very informative face.”

I looked at Jorren.

He nodded.

“What did it say?”

Jorren considered. “You were about to explain why folding was correct.”

“That is not a face.”

“It is your face.”

I disliked this game.

I stayed.

By the fifth hand I understood enough to identify the first layer.

The cards mattered.

The visible row mattered.

What people took mattered.

What they declined mattered.

The order mattered.

Bet size mattered.

Speed mattered.

Eye movement mattered.

Posture mattered.

Breathing probably mattered, although trying to monitor breathing in three other people while remembering which towers had already appeared was excessive unless the expected return justified it.

It did not.

Probably.

Octavia won four bits from the man across from her by looking bored.

I watched carefully.

She did not look bored.

She performed bored.

The distinction was small enough that I only noticed because I had been watching her before she received the card that changed her hand.

Her shoulders had been loose.

Then they became loose on purpose.

Interesting.

The next hand I received two birds, a six of cups, and a useless tower.

Not useless objectively.

Useless to me.

The center row offered another bird.

I took it immediately.

Octavia glanced at me.

Mistake.

Not taking the bird. The speed.

I had announced that I liked it.

I could correct that.

On the next exchange, I waited.

Not naturally. I counted to three.

One.

Two.

Three.

Then I took a card I did not care about.

Octavia's mouth moved.

Not a smile.

Worse.

Recognition.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You did something.”

“I breathed.”

“You breathed judgmentally.”

Jorren said, “She does.”

Octavia flicked one copper bit into the center.

The man across from her matched.

The woman beside him folded.

I matched.

I had a good hand.

Not excellent.

Good enough that the probability depended heavily on what Octavia had hidden, which meant the probability did not actually depend on what she had hidden because I did not know it.

This was the problem with probability when people used it conversationally. They usually meant confidence wearing arithmetic's coat.

Octavia exchanged one card.

Slowly.

I watched her fingers.

Nothing.

Her eyes.

Nothing.

Her shoulders.

Loose.

Naturally loose or deliberately loose?

I had one useful piece of evidence.

She had noticed me trying to manipulate timing.

Therefore she knew I was thinking about behavior.

Therefore any behavior she showed me might be chosen.

Which meant I needed to model what she believed I believed about what she believed I was trying to observe.

No.

That road ended in old men writing books about poker.

I had read some of those books.

Most were terrible.

Different game.

Same disease.

I looked at my cards.

Three birds.

Good.

I put in another bit.

Octavia matched.

The other man folded.

Now it was us.

She looked at me.

I looked back.

There was an obvious move available.

Appear uncertain.

I knew how to appear uncertain because I was uncertain almost constantly.

The difficulty was appearing uncertain in the correct way.

Actual uncertainty made me look at variables.

Performed uncertainty should probably look at the money.

I looked at the money.

Octavia said, “There.”

“What?”

“That.”

“What?”

“You moved your eyes.”

“Eyes move.”

“Not like that.”

I stared at her.

She grinned.

“You're pretending.”

“I am playing cards.”

“Yes.”

“That seems included.”

“It is.”

I considered the problem.

Then I realized I had stopped considering the hand.

This was probably also information.

I pushed in another bit.

Octavia did not.

She folded.

I won.

I felt immediate satisfaction.

Then suspicion.

“You folded because I had the better hand?”

“Yes.”

“Not because of the eye thing.”

“The eye thing told me you wanted me to think you were weak.”

“That should imply strength.”

“Usually.”

“So why fold?”

“Because your first bird was fast.”

I looked at the discarded row.

The first bird.

Five exchanges ago.

She had retained it.

Not the card. The fact.

“You knew I wanted birds.”

“I knew you were pleased by one.”

“That is not the same.”

“No.”

“But enough.”

“For that hand.”

I looked at Jorren.

He was smiling into his cup.

“This game is stupid.”

“Yes,” he said.

I played again.

The next hand I decided not to manipulate anything.

This lasted perhaps twelve seconds.

Then the man across from me raised, and I deliberately scratched my jaw because I had once read that inexperienced gamblers touched their faces when uncomfortable.

Octavia laughed so hard she had to put her cards down.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That is obviously something.”

“You scratched.”

“My face itched.”

“No, it didn't.”

“You cannot know that.”

“You looked at me first.”

I had.

Damn.

The man across from me folded.

“Why did you fold?”

He shrugged. “Didn't like mine.”

“You weren't reacting to me?”

“No.”

This was insulting.

I lost that hand to Octavia.

I lost the next one because I spent too much attention deciding whether the woman beside her was genuinely impatient or performing impatience and failed to notice that I had discarded the only tower that would have protected my pair.

“Cards,” Octavia said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I am learning.”

“You're studying the room.”

“The room is playing.”

“The cards are also playing.”

“The cards are cardboard.”

“They're beating you.”

Jorren made a small choking noise into his cup.

I pointed at him. “You are not participating.”

“I know.”

“You don't get to enjoy this.”

“I paid for the cup.”

“That does not include me.”

“It does today.”

Nessa called, “Table fee.”

I looked at her.

She held up one finger.

“No.”

“Outstanding balance.”

“You stole a copper yesterday.”

“Collected.”

“You invented the fee after I earned the money.”

“Administrative timing.”

Octavia said, “She's very powerful.”

“I have noticed.”

Nessa smiled without warmth.

I returned to the game.

The next hand, I got nothing useful.

Not secretly useful.

Actually bad.

A two of cups, a three of nails, a four of towers, and a seven of birds with no useful relationship between them.

I exchanged.

Still bad.

Again.

Worse.

The rational choice was to fold.

I knew this.

Octavia knew I knew this.

The others probably knew because I had spent the first three hands asking about expected losses from staying in.

I looked at my cards.

Then at Octavia.

She was watching me.

Not the hand.

Me.

I put in one bit.

Her eyebrows rose.

Interesting.

The man across from her folded.

The woman matched.

Octavia matched.

I exchanged my three of nails for a five of cups.

Still bad.

The woman took a tower.

Octavia declined the row entirely.

I put in another bit.

Now Octavia looked at my hands.

Not my face.

My hands.

I kept them still.

This was easier seated. There were advantages to having fewer available dramatic movements.

The woman folded.

Octavia stayed.

Of course she did.

We reached the last exchange.

I took nothing.

Octavia took nothing.

I had a terrible hand.

I pushed in two bits.

Jorren lowered his cup.

Octavia stared at me.

I had intended to look calm.

That was impossible because I was having fun.

Apparently those were different expressions.

She looked at the center.

At me.

At my cards.

At the discarded row.

Then she folded.

For half a second I did not move.

Then I collected the bits.

Octavia pointed at me. “Show.”

“No.”

“Show.”

“Rules say I don't have to.”

“I know the rules.”

“Then this seems resolved.”

“Greg.”

“No.”

Jorren said, “Don't.”

Octavia looked at him.

He shrugged. “He'll become unbearable.”

“I am already unbearable.”

“Worse.”

Octavia leaned back.

“Fine.”

I gathered the bits carefully.

My heart was beating faster than it had any right to.

Not fear.

Not exactly.

The peculiar bodily excitement of having stepped off a ledge that was only one inch high.

I had lied.

Badly, probably.

But successfully.

No.

Not lied.

Represented.

Also no.

I had made a choice intended to alter another person's model of my hand.

That was lying.

Cards made ethics conveniently cheap.

I smiled.

Octavia saw it.

“You had garbage.”

I said nothing.

Her eyes narrowed.

I waited.

This was difficult.

The urge to explain arrived immediately.

I wanted to tell her exactly why the hand had worked, which observations had mattered, which had not, why I had stayed in despite negative expected value, and why her attention shifting from my face to my hands had convinced me that she was uncertain enough to push.

I wanted to explain that the bluff had not been a general success. It had been local. Against her. In that hand. After I had established a pattern of overanalysis and obvious behavioral manipulation.

I wanted to explain all of it.

I did not.

Octavia's eyes narrowed further.

“Oh, fuck you.”

I laughed.

Jorren slapped the table once.

Nessa looked over.

“What?” Nessa asked.

“He didn't explain,” Jorren said.

Nessa frowned. “Is he sick?”

“I can explain.”

Octavia pointed at me. “No.”

The prohibition made it much harder.

I sat there with the explanation pressing against my teeth.

This was absurd.

Then Octavia started laughing.

Not because of the bluff.

Because she could see me suffering.

“You're awful,” I said.

“Yes.”

We played another hand.

I lost.

Then another.

Lost that too.

The bluff had not unlocked secret mastery.

This was disappointing but probably healthy.

By the time Lyssa came through the green door, I was down three bits overall and had developed a completely unjustified hatred of the four of towers.

She stopped beside the table.

“What are you doing?” Lyssa asked.

“Losing,” I said.

Octavia said, “Learning to lie.”

Lyssa looked at me.

I said, “That description lacks context.”

Octavia made a delighted sound.

Lyssa pulled out the empty chair beside me.

“I want the context.”

“You cannot have it.”

She sat.

“Why?”

“I am practicing.”

“Lying?”

“Not explaining.”

She looked at Octavia.

Octavia nodded solemnly.

Lyssa looked back at me.

“How's it going?”

“Poorly.”

“Why?”

I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

Lyssa smiled.

“That badly?”

“Yes.”

She stayed for three hands.

She did not play.

She watched.

This was worse than Octavia watching because I cared what Lyssa thought and because I had recently kissed her enough times to make her opinion physically salient.

I received a pair of cups.

Good enough to stay.

I exchanged once.

Improved.

Octavia watched my face.

I ignored her.

Lyssa watched my cards only when I tilted them enough for her to see, which was probably accidental until I noticed her doing it, at which point it became impossible to know.

I won one bit.

“Very impressive,” Lyssa said.

“Thank you.”

“Was that lying?”

“No.”

“Could've fooled me.”

I looked at her.

She smiled.

I liked her.

This was inconvenient.

The game continued.

My right shoulder began to ache from holding the cards too high.

That was ridiculous.

I lowered them.

My residual limb was fine. My hands were fine. My right leg had started to stiffen from sitting, so I shifted it forward and back under the table.

No catastrophe.

No revelation.

Just body.

After another hand, Lyssa stood.

“I have to go.”

“Where?”

“Work.”

“Oh.”

She looked at me.

I realized the question had sounded disappointed.

I was disappointed.

That was allowed.

Probably.

“I'll see you later?” she asked.

“Yes.”

No model.

No calendar check.

No calculation of whether later meant tonight or tomorrow or an unspecified socially acceptable interval.

Yes.

She bent and kissed my cheek.

Octavia made a noise.

Lyssa pointed at her without looking.

“Don't.”

Octavia raised both hands.

Lyssa left.

I watched the door for slightly too long.

Then I looked back at my cards.

Octavia was smiling.

“No.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You were going to.”

“I was breathing.”

“Judgmentally.”

Jorren said, “She does.”

I lost another bit.

Eventually my shoulder moved from complaint to warning.

Not injury.

Enough.

I put my cards down.

“Done.”

Octavia looked at the pile in front of me.

“You're down four.”

“Three.”

“Four.”

“Nessa stole one.”

“Different ledger.”

“Same purse.”

Jorren stood.

“You going?”

“Yes.”

“Guild?”

I considered.

Alden might still be there.

The throwing game might still be there.

My shoulder had already voted.

“No.”

“Home?”

I looked outside.

Late afternoon light had turned the street gold along one edge and dirty gray along the other. A cart rolled past with empty baskets. Two children chased each other around a post. Someone farther down the street was singing badly while hammering something metal.

I did not want to go home yet.

“No.”

Jorren waited.

I waited too.

He shrugged.

“Food?”

“Yes.”

That was enough.

We went to find something fried.

I did not explain why.

This lasted almost six minutes.

Personal record.
CHAPTER 88
THE OCCUPANT

The keeper asked whether I still wanted my room.

This was a reasonable question.

I disliked it immediately.

“What?”

“Your room.”

“I know which room.”

“Good.”

She was standing at the bottom of the stairs with a folded sheet over one arm and a bucket beside her foot. I was sitting at the kitchen table with bread, cheese, and the six-legged clay horse from the night market.

The horse had migrated.

I had not moved it.

This meant the keeper had.

I pointed at it.

“Why is that here?”

“Rent.”

“That is not rent.”

“Decoration fee.”

“You cannot charge me for an object I own.”

“I can charge the object.”

The horse remained silent.

Coward.

The keeper nodded toward the stairs. “You still want it?”

My room.

Upstairs.

Bed. Window. Trunk. Two shirts I did not particularly like. One shirt I did. A stack of paper. A chipped cup. Three objects I had kept because they might become useful and had not yet justified their continued existence.

My life, apparently.

“Yes.”

“You haven't slept there in four nights.”

“Five.”

She waited.

I hated when people let my corrections improve their argument.

“The downstairs room is working,” she said.

“It is storage.”

“You sleep in it.”

“That does not alter its architectural identity.”

“It has a bed.”

“It has boxes.”

“Your upstairs room also has boxes.”

“Fewer.”

She shifted the sheet to her other arm.

“I'm asking because rent comes tomorrow.”

Ah.

Money.

The least philosophical of all forces.

“How much difference?”

She named it.

I knew the amount already. I had been paying it.

That was not what I had asked.

“How much cheaper downstairs?”

She named that too.

I calculated.

Then I stopped.

Then I calculated anyway because refusing arithmetic on principle was stupid.

The difference was not trivial.

It was also not ruinous.

I could keep the upstairs room.

Probably.

Exact purse remained a thing I had avoided reconstructing because the answer changed every time I ate, rode somewhere, lost at cards, bought a blue shirt, or allowed Nessa to invent taxation.

I had enough.

That was a number.

Not a precise one.

Still useful.

The keeper watched my face.

I wondered whether Octavia had permanently damaged my relationship with faces.

“What?”

“You're doing sums.”

“Yes.”

“Want downstairs?”

“No.”

That came out before the rest of the sums finished.

Interesting.

The keeper nodded.

That was all.

No argument.

No warning about stairs.

No speech about practicality.

She picked up the bucket.

I became suspicious.

“You agree?”

“With what?”

“Keeping the room.”

“You pay for it.”

“Yes.”

“So keep it.”

“You just asked whether I wanted it.”

“Yes.”

“And now you have no opinion.”

“I have lots of opinions.”

“About this.”

She considered.

“Your room has better light.”

That was not the opinion I expected.

She started up the stairs.

“Wait.”

She stopped on the second step and looked back.

“I want to go up.”

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She looked at my shoulder.

My right shoulder was better than yesterday. Not perfect. Raising my arm high still produced a dull objection, but normal crutch use had been fine all morning.

She looked lower.

The residual limb had behaved. Dry. Less swollen. No heat. No new redness. The north road had mostly stopped collecting interest.

Then she looked at my face.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are all doing that now.”

“Doing what?”

“Looking at my face.”

“I've always looked at your face.”

“Not analytically.”

“I promise I am not doing that.”

“That sounds like something someone doing it would say.”

She went upstairs.

I finished breakfast.

Not because she had won.

Because stair practice immediately after eating bread too fast was a poor decision.

There were fourteen steps.

Twelve, landing, two.

The rail ran ash-smooth beneath my left hand, three posts, wall return. Lerris Vane had built it properly. The stringer had been inspected. Nothing was secretly waiting to kill me.

This was useful to remember because my body had developed opinions about stairs independent of engineering.

The keeper came back down with the old sheet.

“You still going?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop staring.”

“I am assessing.”

“You know the stairs.”

“That does not eliminate assessment.”

“It has been seven minutes.”

I stood.

Crutches first.

Right foot planted.

Left knee bent, residual limb clear.

The ascent had become familiar enough to have sequence but not familiar enough to become automatic. That was probably good. Automatic was where my missing foot occasionally rejoined the workforce without authorization.

I put one crutch where I wanted it, hand to rail, weight through right leg, then up.

Pause.

Reset.

Again.

The first four were easy.

Easy was relative.

Easy meant I did not have to negotiate with each muscle individually.

By six, my right thigh was working.

By eight, my left hand had tightened on the rail.

At ten, the keeper said, “Slow.”

“I am slow.”

“Slower.”

This was insulting because she was correct.

I stopped.

Not dramatically.

Just stopped.

My right leg trembled once, then settled.

The old version of me would have categorized the tremor.

Fatigue.

Motor control.

Load.

Recovery interval.

Potential failure mode.

The current version did all of that too.

He was not dead.

He had simply acquired a chair-shaped appreciation for pauses.

There was no chair.

I leaned into the rail and crutch.

The missing left foot felt planted one step below me.

It was not.

I looked down at the actual geometry.

Right foot.

Wood.

Crutch.

Rail.

No left foot.

Good.

“Ready?” the keeper asked.

“Yes.”

Two more.

Landing.

Turn.

The turn remained stupid.

Stairs should not require choreography.

Two final steps.

Then upstairs.

I stood in the narrow hall breathing harder than fourteen steps deserved.

The keeper did not comment.

This was kindness.

Or boredom.

Either was acceptable.

My room smelled closed.

Wood, old cloth, a little dust, the faint dry smell of paper.

The window was shut.

The bed was made badly.

My trunk sat at the foot of it.

Nothing had happened.

This surprised me.

Not intellectually.

I had not expected burglary, fire, structural collapse, spontaneous fungal occupation, or the development of a small upstairs government.

But unused rooms acquire a strange quality. They stop feeling like places and begin feeling like stored versions of places.

I moved to the bed and sat.

The mattress compressed.

Still mine.

Apparently.

The keeper put the clean sheet on the trunk.

“Need anything?”

“No.”

“Coming down before dinner?”

“Yes.”

She looked at me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That was a look.”

“That was me checking whether you were going to try descending alone.”

“I wasn't.”

“Good.”

She left.

I waited until her steps disappeared.

Then I said, “I could.”

The room did not believe me.

I opened the window.

Carrow entered immediately.

Not the city.

The noise.

Cart wheels.

Someone calling prices.

A dog objecting to something with moral certainty.

Hammering from two streets over.

A woman laughing below.

The smell of bread, smoke, horse, river damp, and something fried badly enough that it might still be worth eating.

My upstairs window had a different city than the downstairs storage room.

This was obvious.

Height changed sightlines.

The storage room had wall, alley feet, and whatever portion of the sky happened to survive between buildings.

Up here I could see roofs.

Not many.

Enough.

A slice of Guild roof farther away.

A chimney with three cracked bricks.

Laundry moving between buildings.

Two birds fighting over something on a gutter.

I sat on the bed and watched them.

One bird won.

The other returned six seconds later.

Poor strategic learning.

I approved.

My papers were where I had left them.

I pulled the stack from the trunk.

Old notes.

Work.

Magic.

Money.

Names.

Questions.

The kind of paper archaeology that could consume an afternoon if I let it.

I found one page from before West River.

A list.

Not important enough to remember writing.

Things to ask Edrin.

A Guild job possibility.

Something about Arlo and Vessa's regulator.

A note to price better paper.

At the bottom:

STAIRS AT LODGING?

I stared at it.

I had apparently once considered stairs a property feature.

Technically they still were.

I turned the page over.

Blank.

Good.

I put it aside.

There were newer notes too.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

I had written those downstairs.

They looked different up here.

Not because the words changed.

Because I had a window.

I moved the papers.

The blue shirt hung from a peg.

I touched it.

Still blue.

Excellent.

Good.

The damaged left boot was not here. Tam had the salvage leather.

My right boot sat under the bed beside nothing.

That arrangement looked wrong.

I looked away.

Then back.

Still wrong.

Fine.

Some wrong things were just true.

I took the right boot out, checked the sole, found nothing requiring attention, and put it back.

The empty space remained.

I considered moving something into it.

No.

That would be worse.

I lay back on the bed.

This was not medically optimal posture for everything.

It was, however, extremely good.

My right shoulder relaxed.

My right leg stretched.

The residual limb rested without pressure.

The ceiling had a water stain shaped like a coastline from a country that did not exist.

Or perhaps did.

My future geographic memory was unreliable enough that I could not safely rule out ceiling countries.

I closed my eyes.

I woke to someone knocking.

Not the door downstairs.

My door.

I opened my eyes.

Light had moved across the floor.

I had slept.

This was unacceptable.

“Who?”

“Me.”

Lyssa.

I sat up too fast.

My residual limb swung.

My missing foot struck the floor.

The sensation was complete enough that my stomach dropped before my eyes corrected it.

Nothing hit.

Nothing hurt.

Old map.

I breathed once.

“Wait.”

I looked at myself.

Hair.

Fine.

Shirt.

Not blue.

Why was I not wearing the blue shirt?

Because I had not expected Lyssa.

This was a weak excuse.

I crutched to the door and opened it.

She stood in the hall with one hand against the wall and a folded paper packet under her arm.

“You're upstairs.”

“Yes.”

“I noticed.”

“How?”

“Stairs.”

“Strong evidence.”

She looked past me.

“I've never seen your room.”

This was true.

That seemed suddenly important.

Not objectively.

Still.

“Do you want to?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

I moved aside.

This required more geometry than the gesture deserved.

Crutch.

Door.

Right foot.

Do not block entry with body.

Do not create dramatic invitation accidentally.

Lyssa entered.

She looked around.

There was not much to look at.

Bed.

Trunk.

Window.

Peg.

Paper.

Cup.

One chair.

The six-legged horse was downstairs, which damaged the room's cultural standing.

“This is nicer,” she said.

“Than storage?”

“Yes.”

“That is an extremely low comparison.”

She went to the window.

I watched her look out.

This was different from looking out myself.

Possibly because she had hair that moved when the air came in.

That was not analytically relevant.

I sat on the bed.

“What is that?”

She held up the paper packet.

“Food.”

“Why?”

“You said I'd see you later.”

“I did.”

“This is later.”

Good.

Very strong system.

She opened the packet.

Fried dough.

Honey.

I stared.

“You brought this upstairs?”

“I carried it.”

I looked at my crutches.

Then at the food.

Then at her.

“Yes,” she said.

“I didn't say anything.”

“You did with your face.”

Octavia had ruined everything.

Lyssa sat beside me.

Not touching at first.

Then our shoulders touched.

My right one complained faintly.

I shifted.

She noticed.

“Throwing?”

“Yes.”

“You went back?”

“No.”

“Cards?”

“Yes.”

“How do cards hurt your shoulder?”

“I was holding them too high.”

She laughed.

I ate fried dough.

Honey got on my thumb.

Lyssa took the piece from my hand and ate the rest.

This was theft.

I permitted it.

We talked about nothing important.

Her work.

A customer who had changed her mind three times about a hem and then blamed the cloth.

A man downstairs who had tried to sell the keeper onions too soft to survive the day.

Jorren's theory that fried fish became health food if eaten while walking.

My counterargument that walking while eating fried fish introduced risk without altering nutrition.

Lyssa rejected both positions.

The light moved.

At some point she put her head against my shoulder.

Left shoulder.

Competent woman.

I looked out the window.

The roofs had gone orange.

I thought about rent.

Not the amount.

The room.

I could have moved downstairs.

Cheaper.

Easier.

More practical.

I had not.

There were reasons.

Privacy.

Light.

Air.

Belongings.

A door that was mine to close.

A place Lyssa had not seen before because it belonged to a part of my life that had become temporarily difficult to reach.

All defensible.

I could make the case.

I did not.

Lyssa said, “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You did a whole thing.”

“I did not.”

“You went quiet.”

“That is allowed.”

“It is.”

I waited.

She waited.

I realized she was not asking.

Good.

I ate another piece of fried dough.

Eventually the keeper called from below.

“Greg!”

“Yes?”

“You coming down?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

I looked at the window.

Then at Lyssa.

“Soon.”

The keeper made a sound that traveled up the stairs and conveyed skepticism without language.

Lyssa smiled.

“You need help?”

“No.”

That answer came too quickly.

I corrected it.

“Not with the stairs. I need her spotting.”

Lyssa nodded.

No offense.

No insistence.

No attempt to become useful.

Also good.

We stood.

I took the crutches.

At the door, Lyssa kissed me.

Not my cheek.

Brief.

Then again, less brief.

My body did not attempt to step anywhere.

Progress.

Or sitting had trained it.

No.

Do not build theory from two kisses and a card game.

She pulled back.

“I'll go first.”

“Why?”

“So I'm not standing behind you on the stairs.”

That was sensible.

I disliked how many people around me were sensible without needing my assistance.

She went down.

The keeper came up to the landing.

I followed with the rail, crutch, right foot, pause.

Descent still required more attention than ascent.

At the landing my right thigh trembled.

I stopped.

Nobody spoke.

Then I continued.

At the bottom, I sat immediately.

Not because I had failed.

Because there was a chair.

The keeper handed me water.

Lyssa took the remaining fried dough.

“Hey.”

“You were busy.”

“That does not transfer ownership.”

“It transferred possession.”

I looked at the keeper.

“Do something.”

“Table fee.”

“This is not a table.”

“Stair fee.”

“You cannot keep inventing fees.”

She smiled.

Lyssa laughed.

I drank the water.

Upstairs, my room remained upstairs.

Fourteen steps away.

Still inconvenient.

Still mine.

Rent due tomorrow.

I would pay it.
CHAPTER 89
THE SUBSTITUTE

Rent took less time than deciding to pay rent.

I gave the keeper the money after breakfast.

She counted it once.

I watched.

She looked up.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You're watching me count.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it is money.”

“You think I steal?”

“Yes.”

She nodded. “Fair.”

Then she put the coins away and handed me a folded scrap of paper.

I looked at it.

“What is this?”

“Guild.”

That was not an answer.

The paper had my name on one side.

GREGORY.

Under it, in smaller writing:

IF HE COMES BY, ASK HIM TO WAIT.

No signature.

No task.

No rate.

No explanation.

I turned it over.

Blank.

“When did this arrive?”

“Morning.”

“Who brought it?”

“Boy.”

“Which boy?”

“One with legs.”

I looked at her.

She looked at me.

“That was unnecessary.”

“I thought it narrowed it.”

“It did not.”

I put the note in my pocket.

I did not leave immediately.

This was deliberate.

Possibly petty.

Mostly I wanted another piece of bread.

The Guild was busy when I arrived.

Not dramatic busy.

Ordinary busy.

The front hall had six people waiting, two people arguing, one person pretending not to argue while speaking louder than everyone else, and Merrin behind the front desk with three stacks of paper arranged in the particular order of someone who would know if another person moved one sheet half an inch.

He saw me.

“Good.”

“That is unusually welcoming.”

“Sit.”

There was a stool behind the side end of the desk.

I looked at it.

Then at him.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“What am I doing?”

“Nothing.”

“That is rarely paid.”

“It isn't.”

“Then I object more strongly.”

Merrin took a ledger from under the desk.

A man at the front of the line said, “I've been here twenty minutes.”

Merrin said, “Then you know how the line works.”

The man stopped speaking.

Useful skill.

Merrin pointed at the stool.

“I need to go upstairs.”

“For what?”

“Not your business.”

“Then why am I involved?”

“You aren't.”

“This is becoming circular.”

“Sit there. If anyone asks where I am, say upstairs. If anyone hands you anything, do not accept it. If anyone wants a decision, you cannot make one. If anyone says they were told something, tell them to wait.”

“How long?”

“Ten minutes.”

“That is suspiciously specific.”

“Greg.”

I sat.

Merrin left.

The line looked at me.

I looked at the line.

This was a mistake.

Not mine.

Yet.

The stool was acceptable.

No back.

Too high for my left knee to rest comfortably without the residual limb hanging, so I shifted sideways and planted my right foot. Both crutches fit against the desk within reach.

The first man stepped forward.

“I need a replacement token.”

“I cannot make decisions.”

“It isn't a decision.”

“Then why do you need the Guild?”

He stared at me.

I reconsidered.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Where is he?”

“Upstairs.”

“How long?”

“Approximately ten minutes.”

The man looked at the stairs.

Then at me.

“You new?”

“No.”

“Clerk?”

“No.”

“What are you?”

“Temporarily seated.”

The woman behind him laughed.

He did not.

He stepped aside.

The woman came forward.

“I was told to leave this.”

She held out a sealed envelope.

I did not take it.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“I don't need Merrin. I need to leave this.”

“I was specifically told not to accept anything.”

“With you?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I assume experience.”

She looked at the envelope.

Then at me.

Then tucked it back under her arm.

“Fine.”

Good.

Two people successfully not helped.

The third person was easier.

“Where's Merrin?”

“Upstairs.”

“Fine.”

He left.

Excellent.

I began to understand clerical work.

The fourth person ruined it.

He was carrying a wooden tally board with six small brass tags clipped along one edge.

“I need Bay Three released.”

“I cannot make decisions.”

“Merrin already released it.”

“Then it is released.”

“He didn't mark it.”

“Then wait for Merrin.”

“The cart is outside.”

“Still wait.”

“The driver's charging.”

“That sounds unfortunate.”

He stared at me.

I could see the problem.

That was dangerous.

Bay Three was one of the covered receiving bays on the east side. I knew enough about Guild traffic to know that holding a cart outside cost money and blocked street space. If Merrin had actually approved the release and merely failed to mark the board, waiting ten minutes was pointless.

I also knew Merrin had told me not to make decisions.

Very clear.

Almost offensively clear.

The man put the tally board on the desk.

“Look. Vale consignment. Empty return crates. Nothing sealed.”

I looked.

That was also dangerous.

The tags were ordinary brass.

One marked VALE.

One marked RETURN.

One marked BAY 3.

The rest meant less to me.

“If Merrin released it,” I said, “why are you here?”

“Because the yard won't open the chain without the mark.”

“Correctly.”

“Yes.”

“So wait.”

He exhaled through his nose.

“Fine.”

He moved aside.

I felt good.

This lasted eleven seconds.

A girl came through the front door carrying a basket of folded cloth.

Not a child.

Younger than me, probably.

She looked at the line, looked at me, and said, “Where do I put Guild wash?”

I had no idea.

I could infer.

That was worse.

“Wait for Merrin.”

She stared at me.

“With wet cloth?”

I looked at the basket.

It was not wet.

“Is it wet?”

“No.”

“Then yes.”

She stared longer.

“Who are you?”

“Temporarily seated.”

The woman with the envelope laughed again.

The girl put the basket on the floor and sat on it.

Fine.

The next man wanted to know whether a Bronze named Tavin had checked in.

I knew Tavin.

I did not know whether he had checked in.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Can you look?”

“No.”

“You're behind the desk.”

“That has proven misleading.”

“Ledger's right there.”

He pointed.

The ledger was right there.

I looked at it.

Merrin had not told me not to look at the ledger.

He had told me not to accept things or make decisions.

Looking was not deciding.

I reached toward it.

Then stopped.

The man watched my hand.

I thought of Octavia.

Not because this was performance.

Because being watched altered the decision.

If I opened the ledger, I would know whether Tavin had checked in.

Possibly.

If the ledger was current.

If I read the right column.

If Tavin used the same registry for whatever this man meant by checked in.

Knowledge would arrive faster than authority.

That was familiar.

I put my hand back.

“Wait for Merrin.”

The man sighed.

Good.

I was excellent at this.

Then the front door opened and Jorren came in.

He saw me behind the desk.

Stopped.

Looked at the line.

Looked back at me.

“No.”

“I agree.”

“What happened?”

“Merrin went upstairs.”

“And left you?”

“Yes.”

Jorren looked toward the ceiling.

“He's brave.”

“I have made no decisions.”

The Bay Three man said, “He won't even make the one already made.”

Jorren looked at him.

Then at me.

“What one?”

“Do not assist.”

“I wasn't.”

“Good.”

Jorren smiled.

I disliked him.

He moved to the side wall and leaned against it.

“What do you need?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Now? This.”

He folded his arms.

Spectator.

Traitor.

The line advanced through attrition rather than service.

One person left.

Two more arrived.

A woman asked whether the Guild bought damaged spearheads.

“Wait for Merrin.”

A man asked whether the east yard was open.

I knew it was.

I had seen carts entering when I arrived.

“Yes.”

He thanked me and left.

Jorren said, “Decision.”

“That was observation.”

“You answered.”

“He asked a factual question.”

“What if the yard closed after you came in?”

I looked toward the door.

It had been perhaps fifteen minutes.

No.

Twelve.

Maybe.

“Then I would be wrong.”

“Yes.”

“That does not make it a decision.”

“Feels like one if he gets there and it's shut.”

I hated this.

The girl sitting on the wash basket said, “East yard's open.”

“Thank you.”

“My sister's there.”

“Excellent.”

Jorren nodded. “Now you have a source.”

“I had a source.”

“You had a memory.”

I looked at him.

“Why are you here?”

He smiled.

I looked away.

Merrin still had not returned.

Ten minutes had become something else.

I considered going upstairs.

Impossible.

Not physically impossible.

Administratively impossible.

Leaving the desk defeated the purpose of being at the desk.

Also stairs.

No.

The Bay Three man tapped his tally board.

“Cart's still charging.”

“I know.”

“You could send someone upstairs.”

I looked at the line.

No one volunteered.

Jorren remained useless.

“Go get him,” I said.

The Bay Three man blinked.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

“I can't go upstairs.”

“Why?”

“Yard boots.”

I looked down.

Mud.

Substantial mud.

Guild front hall had rules about that.

Fine.

I looked at Jorren.

“No,” he said.

“I did not ask.”

“You looked.”

“That is apparently legally binding now.”

The woman with the envelope said, “I'll go.”

I looked at her shoes.

Clean.

“Good.”

She started toward the stairs.

Then stopped.

“Can I leave this with you while I go?”

She held out the envelope.

“No.”

She laughed.

“Worth trying.”

She went upstairs carrying it.

This was delegation.

Probably.

I had not made a decision about Guild business.

I had made a decision about who could climb stairs.

No.

She had volunteered.

Important distinction.

The front door opened again.

A man came in fast enough that the room changed.

Not running.

Purposeful.

He went straight to the desk.

“Who has west shed keys?” he asked.

I did not know.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Can't.”

“Why?”

“Latch broke. Door's swinging into the lane.”

That was different.

“How bad?”

“Bad enough I came inside.”

Useful scale.

“Is anyone holding it?”

“Yes.”

“Then wait.”

“They need the keys.”

I looked around.

Everyone was looking at me.

Of course.

I could solve this.

Not the latch.

The information.

Keys had locations.

People knew locations.

The Guild was a system.

I knew enough of it to route a question.

Merrin upstairs.

Yard staff outside.

Jorren standing against wall because he was a bad person.

“Jorren.”

“No.”

“This is not clerical.”

“What is it?”

“Door.”

He looked at the man.

“West shed?”

“Yes.”

“Keys hang in the yard office.”

The man turned.

Then paused.

“Which hook?”

Jorren shrugged. “Ask yard.”

The man left.

Solved.

Not by me.

Annoying.

I felt the shape of the error before I knew what it was.

I had assumed the front desk was the information center because the desk looked like the center.

Jorren knew because he worked here.

The yard knew because they used the keys.

Merrin might not have been necessary at all.

The next person stepped forward.

I held up a hand.

“Before you speak, is there someone other than Merrin who actually owns your problem?”

The man considered.

“Probably.”

“Excellent.”

He left.

Jorren laughed.

“This is much better.”

“I am improving throughput.”

“You're sending everyone away.”

“Those can be identical under certain conditions.”

The girl on the wash basket raised her hand.

I pointed at her.

“Who owns wash?”

“Kitchen.”

“Why are you here?”

“Kitchen told me front hall.”

“Why?”

She shrugged. “They don't want the basket in the kitchen.”

I stared.

System failure.

Or family dynamics.

Impossible to distinguish.

“Wait for Merrin.”

She lowered her hand.

The woman returned from upstairs.

“Merrin says he's coming.”

“Did he say when?”

“No.”

“Did you ask?”

“No.”

I closed my eyes.

She put the envelope on the desk.

I opened my eyes.

“No.”

“You didn't accept it.”

“It is touching the desk.”

“Not your hands.”

“That is not the standard.”

“What standard?”

“Merrin's.”

“He said don't accept it?”

“Yes.”

“You didn't.”

I looked at the envelope.

Then at her.

She smiled.

Octavia had contaminated the population.

I did not touch it.

Merrin returned three minutes later.

He came down the stairs carrying a narrow ledger and looking more annoyed than when he left.

He stopped at the bottom.

Looked at the line.

Looked at me.

Looked at the envelope.

“I didn't accept it,” I said.

The woman said, “True.”

Merrin picked it up.

He looked at the Bay Three tally board.

“Why is this still here?” Merrin asked.

The man made a sound I would have enjoyed if it were not aimed partly at me.

“You told me not to make decisions.”

“I released Bay Three before I went upstairs.”

“He said that.”

“So?”

“You didn't mark it.”

Merrin stared at me.

I stared back.

“Could I have marked it?”

“No.”

“Could I have told the yard to release it?”

“No.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

“Because you could've sent him to Dena.”

I stopped.

“Dena can mark it?”

“She owns bay board when I'm off desk.”

I looked at the Bay Three man.

He looked exhausted.

“Did you know that?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Why didn't you go to Dena?”

“She was in south yard.”

“Why didn't you say that?”

“You didn't ask.”

I looked at Jorren.

He was enjoying himself too much.

Merrin marked the board.

The man took it and left at speed.

Merrin pointed at the wash basket.

“Kitchen.”

“They sent her here.”

Merrin looked at the girl.

“Why?”

“Cook says front hall keeps losing cloth.”

Merrin's face changed.

Not much.

Enough.

“Put it behind the counter.”

I moved my crutch.

The girl slid the basket behind the counter.

Done.

Merrin handled the replacement token in less than a minute.

The damaged spearhead question went to stores.

The Tavin question went to a different registry, not the ledger I had almost opened.

Good.

Very good.

The east yard was still open.

I retained that victory.

Within six minutes, the line was gone.

Merrin sat in his chair.

I remained on the stool.

Jorren remained against the wall.

“Why did you need me?” I asked.

Merrin opened the narrow ledger.

“Because someone had to tell people I was upstairs.”

“That did not require this.”

I gestured at the desk.

“You made it require this.”

“I followed your instructions.”

“Mostly.”

“I made no decisions.”

“You sent a woman upstairs.”

“She volunteered.”

“You told a man to find someone who owned his problem.”

“That was excellent.”

“It was.”

I paused.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

That was suspicious.

Merrin wrote something.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“What are you writing?”

“Work.”

“About me?”

“No.”

I leaned.

He closed the ledger.

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

I sat back.

My right shoulder was fine.

My right thigh had stiffened from the high stool.

The residual limb did not like hanging, so I had kept the knee bent and shifted sideways for most of the time. Not painful. Not ideal.

I stood carefully.

Crutches under arms.

No.

Not under arms.

Hands.

Always hands.

I had corrected that enough times in my head that it had become irritating.

Jorren pushed off the wall.

“You done clerking?”

“I was never clerking.”

Merrin said, “Correct.”

“Thank you.”

“You'd be terrible.”

I looked at him.

“You left me there.”

“For ten minutes.”

“It was thirty.”

“Twenty-seven.”

“That is not better.”

“Upstairs took longer.”

“What was upstairs?”

“Not your business.”

Still.

Good.

I liked that less than I respected it.

I looked at the empty front hall.

There was an obvious conclusion available.

Something about knowing the system from the outside versus knowing who held authority inside it.

Something about desks creating false centers.

Something about questions belonging to people before they belonged to procedures.

Something about how quickly I had wanted to become useful when my assigned task had been to say one sentence and wait.

All true.

Probably.

I did not need all of them.

“What do I get?” I asked.

Merrin looked up.

“For what?”

“Twenty-seven minutes.”

“You sat.”

“I performed queue control.”

“You obstructed queue control.”

“I prevented unauthorized decisions.”

“By you.”

“Exactly.”

Jorren said, “Pay him.”

Merrin looked at him.

“Why?”

“I want to see what number he argues with.”

I considered this.

“Never mind.”

Jorren's face fell.

Excellent.

I turned toward the door.

Merrin said, “Greg.”

I looked back.

He tossed something.

Bad choice.

My right hand was on the crutch.

My left hand was also occupied.

The object hit my chest and dropped.

I stared at the floor.

One copper bit.

Jorren started laughing.

Merrin said, “Substitute clerk.”

“I was not a clerk.”

“Then give it back.”

I bent badly.

Stopped.

No.

I was not picking a copper off the floor while holding two crutches with two people watching.

Jorren picked it up.

He held it out.

I took it.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

Merrin had already returned to his ledger.

I put the bit in my pocket.

One bit was not enough to matter.

That was not the point.

I had been paid for sitting somewhere I did not belong, answering almost nothing, and eventually learning to redirect questions toward people who knew more than I did.

There were worse professions.

I went outside.

The east yard was still open.

I checked.
CHAPTER 90
THE BUYER

I wanted a chair.

Not a special chair.

This distinction became important.

I wanted an ordinary wooden chair with four legs, a back, a seat, and no moral purpose.

The chair in my upstairs room had all of those things except comfort.

Comfort had not mattered much before because I had mostly used it for putting clothes on.

Now I was spending more time upstairs.

Reading.

Writing.

Looking out the window.

Occasionally allowing a woman to bring me fried dough.

The chair had developed ambitions beyond its construction.

After twenty minutes, the front edge pressed behind my right thigh. After thirty, my lower back began negotiating. The left side of the seat did nothing useful for the residual limb, which was not the chair's fault because the chair had been built for a customer with the standard inventory of lower legs.

Still.

I wanted a better chair.

This was how I ended up in a furniture shop arguing against improvements.

The shop sat three streets east of the lodging house, open to the road through a pair of wide doors. Half the front room was chairs. The other half was tables pretending not to be chairs.

Wood shavings curled across the floor.

A woman at a workbench was fitting a stretcher between two chair legs.

I knew her by face.

She knew me by face.

This was increasingly common in Carrow and mildly alarming.

“You're the stair rail,” she said.

“I am not.”

“The one with the rail.”

“Yes.”

“Lerris made it.”

“Yes.”

She looked at my crutches.

Then at me.

“Chair?”

“Yes.”

She stood.

I immediately became suspicious.

“Ordinary chair.”

She stopped.

“I haven't said anything.”

“I am establishing scope.”

“Sit.”

She pointed to a chair.

I sat.

It was too low.

“Not that one.”

“You told me to sit.”

“I was learning.”

“About me?”

“About the chair.”

Good answer.

I stood.

This took more effort than I wanted it to.

Low chairs were traps disguised as furniture.

Right foot under me.

Hands.

Push.

Crutch.

Balance.

The woman watched.

I disliked that.

Not because she was staring.

Because she was competent enough that I could see her measuring without measuring.

“How high's yours?”

I told her approximately.

She held a hand beside her hip.

“That?”

“Probably.”

“Probably is bad furniture.”

“I can measure it.”

“Do that.”

She moved to another chair.

Higher.

Flat seat.

Straight back.

Arms.

“No arms.”

“Why?”

“They interfere with crutches.”

“Getting up?”

“Sometimes. Also placing them beside me.”

She looked at the chair.

Then moved it away without argument.

Excellent.

Third chair.

No arms.

Higher seat.

Slight backward angle.

I sat.

Better.

Not good.

The front edge still met my right thigh in the wrong place.

I shifted.

She watched.

“What?”

“You're sitting crooked.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I looked down.

My left knee was bent. The residual limb stayed clear of the seat edge, but to do that comfortably I had rotated slightly right.

“Because if I sit square, the left side presses here.”

I touched the back of my thigh above the knee.

“Not the end?”

“No.”

She nodded.

This was good.

No dramatic pause.

No expression about tragedy.

Just location.

She crouched and looked at the seat.

“Could cut the left front corner back.”

“No.”

She looked up.

“Why?”

“I want a chair.”

“That would still be a chair.”

“I want an ordinary chair.”

“Ordinary chairs fit ordinary bodies badly all the time.”

“That is not helping your sales argument.”

“It is helping my chair argument.”

I stood.

She moved to a fourth.

“Try.”

I did.

This one had a woven seat.

Higher again.

The weave gave slightly under my weight.

Better on the right thigh.

Worse under the left because the edge sagged differently when I shifted.

“No.”

She nodded.

Fifth.

Wood.

Broad seat.

Almost level.

Back upright enough that I could write at a table without folding forward.

I sat square.

Interesting.

The seat was deep enough that the left thigh rested without the front edge reaching the sensitive area behind the knee. The residual limb hung free without contact.

My right foot planted.

I could stand from it without using the back of my right calf against the seat.

I stood.

Sat.

Stood again.

The woman said, “That's annoying.”

“What?”

“You found one.”

“You wanted me to find one.”

“I wanted to sell you work.”

“Ah.”

She was honest.

I liked her.

This was dangerous.

“How much?”

She named a price.

I disliked her.

“That is a chair.”

“Yes.”

“Not a horse.”

“No.”

“It has four legs and no ability to move itself.”

“Correct.”

“That should reduce cost.”

“Horse eats.”

“This does not.”

“Exactly.”

I looked at the chair.

Good chair.

Too expensive.

Not impossibly expensive.

More than I wanted to spend.

“How much for the ugly one?”

She looked around.

“Which ugly one?”

I pointed.

A chair near the wall had a broad seat, one repaired back spindle, and a dark stain across one side that looked like someone had died while eating stew.

“That isn't ugly.”

“It is visibly guilty.”

“Old tavern chair.”

“Why is it here?”

“Repair.”

“For the tavern?”

“No. They replaced the set. I bought six.”

“How many left?”

“Two.”

“Why?”

“Because they're good chairs.”

I crutched over.

She moved it clear for me.

I sat.

The seat was broad.

Height good.

Back slightly too curved.

The repaired spindle did not matter.

The stain was definitely stew.

Probably.

I shifted left.

No edge pressure.

Right foot planted.

I stood.

Easy enough.

“How much?”

She named a lower price.

Still not low.

“Why is the new one so much more?”

“New wood. New labor. Matching stock. Finish.”

“This has labor.”

“Repair labor.”

“And old wood.”

“Yes.”

“Which has survived long enough to demonstrate structural competence.”

She stared at me.

“That is the worst way anyone has ever asked for a discount.”

“It is a valid point.”

“No.”

“Old furniture has evidence.”

“Old furniture has old joints.”

“Which you repaired.”

“One spindle.”

“What about the joints?”

“Checked.”

“So evidence.”

She folded her arms.

I had become a customer.

This was different from being useful.

I had no jurisdiction.

No professional standing.

No reason she should care what I thought except that I had money and she wanted some of it.

This was refreshing.

“How much if I carry it?”

She looked at my crutches.

I looked at the chair.

“That was a test.”

“You failed it.”

“I agree.”

“Delivery's one bit.”

“One bit?”

“Three streets.”

“I can see my lodging from the corner.”

“Then carry it.”

I looked at her.

She smiled.

Octavia had also ruined smiles.

“Half bit.”

“There is no half bit.”

“Then free.”

“One bit.”

“I will ask Jorren.”

“Then Jorren can carry it.”

“He might.”

“Good.”

This was not going well.

I stood beside the chair.

I wanted it.

This fact had become irritatingly simple.

There were other chairs.

I could keep using the one upstairs.

I could ask the keeper whether there was another chair somewhere in the lodging house.

I could buy nothing.

I could wait.

I could spend the money.

The chair was not an investment.

It would not increase earning capacity in any defensible way.

It would not unlock a professional category.

It was not medical equipment.

It was not magical.

It was not even attractive.

It was comfortable.

I sat again.

Yes.

Damn.

“I'll take it.”

The woman nodded.

“One bit delivery.”

“I object.”

“Noted.”

“I am not paying delivery.”

“Then don't.”

“I want the chair.”

“Then solve your problem.”

I stared at her.

She returned to the workbench.

Conversation over.

I sat in my purchased chair while she worked.

This was strange.

I had not paid yet.

Possession was conceptually unstable.

“Can I leave it here?”

“For how long?”

“Until I find someone to carry it.”

“Today.”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

“What if tomorrow?”

“Storage fee.”

“You people are inventing fees.”

“Who is people?”

“Nessa. Keeper. You.”

She tapped the floor beside the chair.

“Chair can stay today. Tomorrow, the floor costs.”

Possibly.

I paid for the chair.

Not delivery.

Principle mattered.

Then I left to find Jorren.

He was not at the Guild.

This was inconvenient but reasonable because Jorren did not exist to transport my furniture.

Alden was there.

Worse.

He was coming out of the side yard with a practice shield under one arm and sweat darkening his shirt.

He saw me.

“Game?”

“No.”

He looked offended.

“I bought a chair.”

His expression changed.

“What?”

“I need to move a chair.”

“Why?”

“Because I bought it.”

“Why?”

“To sit.”

He stared.

This was fair.

“Where?”

I told him.

“Where to?”

“Lodging.”

He looked at my crutches.

“Yes,” I said.

“I didn't say anything.”

“You did.”

“With my face?”

“Everyone is doing this now.”

Alden laughed.

“I have training.”

“Now?”

“In a little.”

“How little?”

He looked toward the yard.

“Enough to carry a chair?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“What?”

“You will be late.”

“I can carry a chair three streets.”

“I believe you.”

“Then?”

“I do not want Pessa arriving at my lodging to kill me because I converted your training time into furniture logistics.”

“She won't kill you.”

“Good.”

“She'll make me run.”

“Worse.”

Alden considered.

“After?”

“When?”

“After training.”

“That is an actual time category?”

“No.”

“Excellent.”

He went back inside.

I stood outside the Guild.

I could wait.

I did not want to wait.

This was partly because the chair was mine now and remained somewhere else.

Ownership creates ridiculous urgency.

I went to the green door.

Octavia was not there.

Nessa was.

“Jorren's not here.”

“I haven't asked.”

“You looked for him before you looked at the bar.”

“Fuck all of you.”

She laughed.

“Jorren?”

“Not here.”

“Sevren?”

“Road.”

“Octavia?”

“Freight office.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you here?”

“I was checking.”

“For people.”

“Yes.”

“Very moving.”

I left.

I considered the freight office.

No.

Octavia had work.

Sevren had work.

Jorren had somewhere he was not.

Alden had training.

Lyssa had work.

This was becoming a survey of other people's schedules.

Good.

Healthy.

Annoying.

I went back to the furniture shop.

The woman looked up.

“No porter?”
